model_plain: Most Texans vote in person, either during early voting (Oct. 19 to 30) or on Election Day (Nov. 3). Mail ballots are only for people who qualify: 65 or older, sick or disabled, out of the county, expecting a baby, or in jail.

deadlines.rule: Texas has no online voter registration. You can fill out the form online at VoteTexas.gov, but you must print, sign and mail it, or you can update an existing registration's address online. The deadline for all methods was Monday, October 5, 2026.
Mailed applications had to be postmarked on or before Monday, October 5, 2026 (30 days before the election).
In-person applications at the county voter registrar's office or a volunteer deputy registrar were due Monday, October 5, 2026.

registration.same_day_notes: Texas does not have same-day registration. You cannot register during early voting or on Election Day.
registration.still_possible_now: No. The deadline to register for the November 3 election was Monday, October 5, 2026, and it has passed. If you registered before then, confirm it worked at the My Voter Portal (link above). If you moved to a new Texas county and didn't re-register there by October 5, you may be able to vote a 'limited ballot' (only the races your old and new county share) at your new county's main early voting location, during early voting only, not on Election Day. If you moved within the same county, you can still vote: go to a polling place and fill out a Statement of Residence.

mail_ballot.who_gets_one: You must apply, and you must qualify. Texas allows voting by mail only if you: are 65 or older on Election Day; are sick or have a disability that keeps you from going to the polls without help or risk to your health; expect to give birth within three weeks before or after Election Day; will be out of your county during all of early voting and on Election Day; or are confined in jail but otherwise eligible. Nobody is mailed a ballot automatically. If you're 65+ or have a disability you can file one 'annual' application that covers every election in the calendar year.

request_deadline.rule: Your application must be received (not postmarked) by your county's Early Voting Clerk by Friday, October 23, 2026. Get the form (6-1f) at VoteTexas.gov or from your county. You can submit it by mail, in person, by fax or by email as a signed scanned attachment, but if you fax or email it the signed original must arrive by mail within 4 business days. The application must include your Texas driver license, personal ID or Election Identification Certificate number (NOT your VUID), or if you have none of those, the last 4 digits of your Social Security number. Send it to the Early Voting Clerk in the county where you're registered.

return_options: mail (USPS) to your county Early Voting Clerk, arriving by 7:00 PM Nov. 3, OR postmarked by 7:00 PM Nov. 3 and arriving by 5:00 PM Wednesday, Nov. 4
common or contract carrier (FedEx, UPS) arriving by 7:00 PM Nov. 3
hand-deliver it yourself, in person, to the county Early Voting Clerk's office, but only on Election Day (Nov. 3) while polls are open, with your photo ID (Election Code 86.006(a-1))
Texas does not use ballot drop boxes
mail_ballot.postage: Varies by county; check your return envelope. Harris County says it takes two standard stamps ($1.10) but that a ballot mailed without postage will still be delivered and counted. We did not find a statewide official statement on postage, so treat this as sourced, not verified: https://www.harrisvotes.com/Voter/Voting-FAQ
mail_ballot.signature_witness_rules: Sign the carrier envelope, and write your ID number in the space provided: your Texas driver license, personal ID or Election Identification Certificate number, or the last 4 of your SSN if DPS never issued you one of those. The number must match what's on your voter registration record. No notary. No witness unless you cannot sign; then a witness signs and prints their name and address. If someone helps you mark or mail the ballot, their name, address and signature must go on the envelope too. Election Code 86.006 and VoteTexas carrier envelope page.
mail_ballot.cure_process: If your mail ballot has an ID, signature or other envelope problem, follow the notice from your county. You can correct an ID number through the Ballot by Mail Tracker if eligible, return the corrective action form, or visit the early voting clerk. The Secretary of State's Nov. 3 election calendar gives Monday, November 9, 2026 as the deadline to correct carrier-envelope defects. Act as soon as you receive a notice. If you switch to voting in person, follow the county's cancellation instructions before voting.
mail_ballot.mail_cutoff_advice: The state says return it 'as soon as possible.' Texas does not set a 'don't mail after' date, but postmarks are unreliable: USPS may not postmark mail the day you drop it in a box. If you're mailing in the last week, take it to a post office counter and ask for a hand postmark (free). Better: if it's Election Day, hand-deliver it to the Early Voting Clerk's office with your photo ID by 7:00 PM.

early_in_person.hours_note: Monday, Oct. 19 through Friday, Oct. 30, including the weekend of Oct. 24 and 25. Hours are set by each county. Travis: every day 7 AM to 7 PM, with some sites open until 10 PM on Oct. 29 and 30. Harris: Mon through Sat 7 AM to 7 PM, Sunday Oct. 25 noon to 7 PM. Dallas: Mon through Sat 7 AM to 7 PM, Sunday Oct. 25 noon to 6 PM. Bexar regular sites: October 19 to 23, 8 AM to 6 PM; October 24, 7 AM to 7 PM; October 25, noon to 6 PM; October 26 to 30, 7 AM to 7 PM. Two branch sites, Bexar County Justice Center and Valley Ranch Community Center, open weekdays only, 8 AM to 6 PM, throughout October 19 to 30. Check your county's site for exact hours at your location.

election_day.in_line_rule: If you are inside or in line at the polling place at 7:00 PM, you get to vote. Stay in line. (Election Code 41.032)

accepted: U.S. military ID card with your photo
U.S. citizenship certificate with your photo
Expiration: if you're 18 to 69, the ID can be expired up to 4 years. If you're 70 or older, it can be expired any length of time. The citizenship certificate never expires.
id_rules.no_id_option: If you don't have one of the seven photo IDs and can't reasonably get one, you can still vote a regular ballot: show a supporting document (voter registration certificate, current utility bill, bank statement, government check, paycheck, certified birth certificate, or any government document with your name and address, copy or original) and sign a Reasonable Impediment Declaration at the polls. If you have none of that, you vote a provisional ballot and have until the 6th day after the election (Monday, Nov. 9, 2026) to bring ID to the county voter registrar's office so it counts (Election Code 65.0541). You can also leave and come back with ID before polls close.

in_the_booth.phones_detail: You may not use a phone or any wireless device inside the room where voting is happening. Texas Election Code 61.014(a), as amended by HB 3909 effective Sept. 1, 2025: 'a person may not use a wireless communication device within a room in which voting is taking place.' Separately, 61.014(b) bans recording images or sound within 100 feet of a voting station. The judge can make you turn it off or leave (61.014(c)). Put your phone away before you walk in. Counties like Harris still tell voters 'within 100 feet,' so expect to be asked to put it away as you approach. Statute: https://statutes.capitol.texas.gov/Docs/EL/pdf/EL.61.pdf
in_the_booth.notes_detail: Yes. Bring paper. The Texas Secretary of State says in writing: 'Voters are allowed to bring written materials into voting stations to assist them in casting their ballot' (Election Advisory 2025-01, April 17, 2025, and the SOS 'Activities in Vicinity of Polling Places' handout). A printed cheat sheet, a marked-up sample ballot or handwritten notes are all fine. Two limits: (1) you can't post or hand out your guide at the polling place, and (2) the election judge can decide a document is 'electioneering' if it's campaign material rather than your personal notes, so keep it to your own list and take it with you when you leave. Harris County puts it plainly: 'What should I bring to vote? Your printed sample ballot or handwritten notes.' Sources: https://www.sos.state.tx.us/elections/laws/advisory2025-01.shtml and https://www.sos.state.tx.us/elections/forms/activities-in-vicinity-polling-places.pdf and https://www.harrisvotes.com/Voter/Election-Information
in_the_booth.apparel_rule: No campaign gear within 100 feet of the door. Election Code 61.010(a) bans wearing a badge, insignia, emblem 'or other similar communicative device' relating to a candidate, measure or party on the ballot, inside the polling place or within 100 feet of an outside door. It's a Class C misdemeanor. The SOS reads this (after the Ostrewich v. Hudspeth judgment) as: apparel about a candidate, measure or party on this ballot is out; apparel about something not on this ballot is OK. Practical advice: wear a plain shirt, or turn a campaign shirt inside out, and leave the hat in the car. The same 100-foot zone bans electioneering of any kind (61.003), and the zone is marked by signs outside the building.

gotchas.text: Registration is closed. The deadline was October 5. If you aren't registered, you can't vote in this election. Check your status at the My Voter Portal before you go so there are no surprises.
gotchas.short: Check your registration before you go; the Oct 5 deadline has passed.

gotchas.text: If you applied for a mail ballot but want to vote in person, bring the mail ballot with you and hand it over ('surrender' it) to get a regular ballot. If you show up without it, you'll have to vote a provisional ballot, which only counts after the county confirms your mail ballot was never returned.
gotchas.short: Bring your mail ballot to the polls if you'd rather vote in person.

gotchas.text: No phones in the voting room, period, and no ballot photos (recording within 100 feet of a voting station is banned, Election Code 61.014). Research at home and bring a printed cheat sheet or handwritten notes. Paper is explicitly allowed; phones are not. The 'I Voted' sticker selfie outside is fine.
gotchas.short: Leave your phone outside the voting room; bring printed or handwritten notes instead.

gotchas.text: A mail ballot arriving after 7 PM on November 3 only counts if it has a postmark by that time AND arrives by 5 PM the next day. Postmarks are not guaranteed; if you're cutting it close, hand-deliver it to the Early Voting Clerk's office on Election Day with your photo ID, or just vote in person.
gotchas.short: Close to Nov 3, hand-deliver your mail ballot with photo ID, or vote in person.

gotchas.text: Vote centers: in Travis, Williamson, Hays, Dallas, Collin, Tarrant, Harris, Fort Bend and Bexar counties you can vote at ANY polling location in your county, during early voting and on Election Day. You are not tied to a precinct. Pick the one with the shortest line.
gotchas.short: In vote-center counties like Travis and Harris, vote at any location in your county.

gotchas.text: For a write-in, use the official declared write-in list for your ballot. It must be posted in each voting booth and included with mail ballots. On paper ballots, a write-in line appears only in races with a declared write-in candidate. The SOS list covers federal, state and district offices; county and precinct write-ins are certified locally.
gotchas.short: For a write-in, pick a name from the official declared write-in list.

situations.question: I moved to a new address in Texas.
situations.short: Same county: vote anywhere with a Statement of Residence; new county: ask about a limited ballot by Oct 30.
situations.answer: If you moved within the same county, you can still vote: go to any polling place in your county and fill out a short Statement of Residence. If you moved to a different Texas county and didn't re-register there by October 5, you may be able to vote a limited ballot in your new county, but only during early voting (Oct 19 to 30) at its main early voting site.
steps: Same county (say, a move within Travis or within Harris): vote anywhere in the county and tell the worker your address changed.
New county (say, Travis to Williamson or Hays): call your new county's early voting clerk before Oct 30. A limited ballot covers only the races your old and new counties share.
Update your address with your county voter registrar so you're set for next time. Same-county moves can be done online at Texas.gov.

situations.question: I just moved to Texas from another state.
situations.short: Texas registration closed Oct 5, so register now for next time.
situations.answer: Texas registration for this election closed October 5, so if you weren't registered here by then, you can't vote in Texas on November 3. Register now so you're ready next time; a registration takes effect 30 days after the county accepts it.
steps: Fill out the form at VoteTexas.gov, then print, sign and mail it to your county voter registrar. Texas has no fully online registration.
Get a Texas driver's license or ID card. Texas asks for photo ID at the polls.

situations.question: I'm not registered to vote.
situations.short: The deadline was Oct 5, but check first, because you may be registered and not know it.
situations.answer: We're sorry: the Texas deadline was October 5, so if you didn't register by then, you can't vote in this election. Before you give up, double-check, because you may be registered and not know it.
steps: Look yourself up at the My Voter Portal, or call your county voter registrar.
Registered but moved within your county? You can still vote. See the moving question.
Truly not registered? Mail in an application now so you're ready for the next election.

situations.question: I went to the wrong polling place.
situations.short: In Travis, Williamson, Hays and Harris, you can vote at any polling place in your county.
situations.answer: Travis, Williamson, Hays and Harris counties use vote centers, so you can vote at any polling place in your county, early or on Election Day. Just head to the closest one in the county where you're registered.
steps: Find locations (and wait times, in many counties) on your county elections site or the My Voter Portal.
In a different county? Go back to your own county; that's where your ballot is.

situations.question: My mail ballot never came, or I lost it.
situations.short: Vote in person instead, or cancel it in writing and apply for a new one by Oct 23.
situations.answer: Texas only mails ballots to voters who applied and qualified. If yours never came or got lost, you can vote in person instead, or cancel it in writing and apply for a new one.
steps: Check the Ballot by Mail Tracker to see whether it was mailed.
To vote in person, sign a cancellation form at the polls. Without the ballot to hand in, you vote a provisional ballot, counted once the county confirms your mail ballot wasn't returned.
Want a new mail ballot? Send your county's early voting clerk a signed cancellation and a new application. It must arrive by Oct 23.

situations.question: I made a mistake on my ballot.
situations.short: Don't cast it; ask a worker for a new one, or bring a mail ballot to the polls and vote.
situations.answer: At the polls, don't cast it: Texas law gives you a new ballot when you hand the spoiled one back to an election worker. On a mail ballot, bring the whole packet to an early voting site or your Election Day polling place, surrender it, and vote in person.
steps: In person: tell a poll worker before you cast your ballot and ask for a new one.
Mail ballot: bring the ballot and envelope with you, so you can vote a regular ballot instead of a provisional one.

situations.question: I mailed my ballot but now want to vote in person.
situations.short: Once the county has it, that's your vote; if you still have it, bring it to the polls and vote.
situations.answer: Once the county has your marked mail ballot, that's your vote and you can't swap it for an in-person one. If you haven't sent it yet, bring it to any polling place in your county, surrender it, and vote a regular ballot.
steps: Check the Ballot by Mail Tracker to see whether it was received.
Still have it? Bring the ballot and envelope with you.
Can't find it? You can still vote in person, but it will be a provisional ballot.

situations.question: I don't have an ID.
situations.short: If you can't get a photo ID, bring a utility bill or bank statement and sign a Reasonable Impediment Declaration.
situations.answer: Texas asks for one of 7 photo IDs, like a Texas driver's license or a U.S. passport, and it can be expired up to 4 years (any length of time if you're 70 or older). If you don't have one and can't reasonably get one, bring a supporting document, like a utility bill, bank statement or your voter registration certificate, and sign a Reasonable Impediment Declaration to vote a regular ballot.
steps: Have a photo ID but left it at home? Go get it and come back before polls close.
Or vote a provisional ballot and show your ID at the county voter registrar's office by Monday, Nov 9.
Student IDs and out-of-state licenses are not on the list.

situations.question: My name changed since I registered.
situations.short: You can still vote if your name is close enough; you sign a short affidavit at the polls.
situations.answer: You can still vote. If the name on your ID doesn't exactly match the voter list, workers check whether it's substantially similar (they also look at your address and birth date), and if it is, you sign a short affidavit and vote.
steps: Bring your photo ID, plus your voter registration certificate if you have it.
Send your county voter registrar an updated registration form so your new name is on file next time.

situations.question: I'm a college student.
situations.short: Vote where you're registered; if that's home and you'll be away, your mail ballot application must arrive by Oct 23.
situations.answer: Registration closed October 5, so you vote where you're already registered. If that's your family's county and you'll be away at school for all of early voting and on Election Day, you can vote by mail, but your application must arrive by Friday, October 23.
steps: Get the mail ballot application at VoteTexas.gov and send it to the early voting clerk in your home county.
Registered at school (say, UT in Travis or Texas State in Hays)? Vote at any polling place in that county.
Voting in person? Bring one of the 7 photo IDs. Student IDs don't count in Texas.

situations.question: I'll be away on Election Day.
situations.short: Vote early at any site in your county through Oct 30.
situations.answer: Vote early in person, Monday, October 19 through Friday, October 30, at any early voting site in your county. If you'll be out of your county for all of early voting and on Election Day, you can vote by mail; your application must arrive by Friday, October 23.
steps: Check your county's early voting hours (Travis, Williamson, Hays and Harris each post their own).
Mail ballot: get the form at VoteTexas.gov and send it to your county's early voting clerk.
A mailed ballot must arrive by 7 PM Nov 3, or be postmarked by then and arrive by 5 PM Nov 4.

situations.question: I'm in line when polls close.
situations.short: Stay in line: if you're in line at 7 PM, you get to vote.
situations.answer: Stay in line. If you're inside or in line at the polling place at 7 PM, you get to vote.
steps: Don't leave, even if the line is long.
Put your phone away before you reach the voting room.

situations.question: They said my signature doesn't match.
situations.short: Fix it by Nov 9 with the Corrective Action Form, by mail or at your county's early voting clerk.
situations.answer: You can fix it. Fill out the Corrective Action Form that came with your notice and mail it back, or do it in person at your county's early voting clerk's office, by Monday, November 9.
steps: If the problem is a missing or wrong ID number, fix it online in the Ballot by Mail Tracker.
Or cancel your mail ballot and vote in person. Without the ballot to hand in, it will be a provisional ballot.
Act the day you get the notice.

situations.question: What's a provisional ballot?
situations.short: It's a backup ballot when workers can't confirm you can vote; the county decides later if it counts.
situations.answer: It's a backup ballot for when workers can't confirm on the spot that you can vote, such as when you're not on the list or don't have ID with you. You sign a short affidavit, and the county decides afterward whether it counts.
steps: If it was about ID, show your photo ID at the county voter registrar's office by Monday, Nov 9.
You'll get a notice in the mail saying whether it counted, and why if it didn't.

situations.question: How do I check my ballot was counted?
situations.short: If you voted by mail, use the Ballot by Mail Tracker; a provisional ballot gets a mailed notice.
situations.answer: If you voted by mail, use the state's Ballot by Mail Tracker to see when your ballot was received and whether there's a problem to fix. If you voted a provisional ballot, the county mails you a notice saying whether it counted.
steps: Log in with your Texas license or ID number and the last 4 of your Social Security number.
If it shows a problem, fix it by Monday, Nov 9.

judicial_review.how_judges_get_here: Texas judges run with party labels. You choose between candidates, rather than voting yes or no on retaining a judge. Governors can appoint judges to fill vacancies between elections.
judicial_review.who_reviews: There is no official job-review commission for these elections. Bar associations sometimes poll lawyers. The State Bar’s 2026 poll covered primary candidates; Houston’s separate general-election poll covers statewide and Houston-area races.
judicial_review.what_the_rating_means: A preference poll counts which candidate responding lawyers prefer. It is different from a commission’s assessment of whether a judge meets job standards.
judicial_review.what_it_doesnt_mean: The bar’s poll is not its endorsement. Only responding lawyers are counted; it is not a poll of all lawyers or all voters.
judicial_review.to_keep_a_judge: Vote for the candidate you want. In the general election, the candidate with the most votes wins the seat.
judicial_review.history: Houston’s 2026 judicial preference poll is available. Statewide primary poll results should not be presented as November general-election ratings.

Bring a paper cheat sheet. You may use written notes, but phones and other wireless devices cannot be used within 100 feet of a voting station.
